newsitem.title: CONGO: Idea of African peace force for Congo floated.
newsitem.headline: Idea of African peace force for Congo floated.

text.p: The Congo Republic's battered capital of Brazzaville has enjoyed a second day of relative calm as mediators focused on ways of halting political and ethnic bloodshed and organising promised presidential elections.

Envoys from President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor and arch rival Denis Sassou Nguesso agreed on Saturday to meet in Gabon to for talks on implementing a peace deal -- with deployment of an African force being touted as one solution.

Confusion surrounded the timing of the talks. Brazzaville mayor and mediator Bernard Kolelas said the envoys would meet on Sunday. Others mediators and sources in Gabon's capital Libreville said the talks would most likely be on Monday.

"We must do everything to ensure that the elections are held within the delays foreseen in the constitution," U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said after talks with all sides. "Democracy must definitely be put back on track," he said.

The conflict erupted on June 5 after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election. Lissouba's mandate ends of August 31.

Despite occasional explosions and shooting in the centre of the oil-producing former French colony's capital on Saturday, a truce declared by both sides on Wednesday at last showed signs of taking hold. Friday too was comparatively quiet.

Bodies litter Brazzaville's streets and the smell of rotting corpses permeates parts of the city. Some sources say the death toll could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand but many of the dead lay uncollected where they fell.
Soldiers supporting Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso's militiamen spent much of the day drinking beer or casually looting.
At Sassou Nguesso's heavily fortified home, one stop on Sahnoun's shuttle around town, a young militiaman held an AK-47 in one hand and a selection of children's toys in the other.

Sahnoun, travelling in an armoured car and protected by French special forces commandos, crossed battle lines in the city, passing buildings smashed by rockets and looters. Fires smouldered in some as dusk closed in.
France, which has evacuated almost 5,000 foreign nationals, about a third of them French, says that it will wind up its rescue mission on Sunday and start pulling out.
Sahnoun said that one idea on the table was for an African peace force. "We are going to discuss this issue," he said. "We don't rule out an African presence."
Lissouba told Gabon-based Africa Number One radio he favoured deployment of an African force, "possibly led by France with whom we are used to working, to guarantee the elections".
Sassou Nguesso, whose Cobra militia made some gains during last week's fighting, said he was not opposed the idea -- "on condition that it (the force) does not become permanent."
He too has called for elections to go ahead. "On the eve of the polling, passions must be cooled and conditions created for fair and transparent elections," he said.

Kolelas was runner-up to Lissouba in a 1992 presidential election. His supporters were in the thick of fighting that killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 after disputed parliamentary elections. This time they have stayed clear.
Sassou Nguesso, named president in 1979, bowed to pressure for multi-party politics in 1990 but was among candidates knocked out in the first round of the 1992 poll.
